ety.text: From Middle English him, from Old English him, from Proto-Germanic *himmai (“to this, to this one”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian him (“him”), West Frisian him (“him”), Sylt North Frisian ham, höm (“him”), Dutch hem (“him”), German Low German hum, hüm, em (“him”), German ihm (“him”, dative).

senses.d: With dative effect or as an indirect object.
ex: […]therfoꝛ Chꝛiſt wold not call him abominable / But the verye abomination it ſilf.
‘I promise,’ he said as I gave him the papers.
She was in no humour for conversation with anyone but himself; and to him she had hardly courage to speak.

senses.d: With accusative effect or as a direct object.
ex: ‘He's got it buttoned in his breast. I saw him put it there.’

senses.d: As a grammatical subject or object when joined with a conjunction.
ex: Now him and Bernie are best friends.
He released a [statement] warning that him and 25,000 troops were going to stage a coup.

senses.d: Used in isolation or apposition, or (sometimes proscribed) as the complement of the copula (be).
ex: Who was there? —Him.
Who did this? —Him. He did it. (or:) It was him. He did it.)
Apon a daye apoynted, the kynge arayed hym in royall apparell, and set hym in his seate, and made an oracion unto them.

senses.d: With nominative effect: he, especially as a predicate after be, or following a preposition.
ex: Before my body, I throw my warlike Shield: Lay on Macduffe, And damn'd be him, that first cries hold, enough.
Lowe quit the West Wing last year amid rumours that he was unhappy that his co-stars earned more than him.

senses.d: A person of elevated skill at a sport, game, or other activity.
ex: Stop trying that, you're not him bro.
Bro thinks he's him.
I think this bird is a him, but it may be a her.
[…] daring dizzying passages in other, fleeting and passionate dwellings within the hims and hers whom she inhabits […]

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish lo (“the; him; it”). As a masculine pronoun, from Latin illum, the accusative masculine singular of ille (“that, that one”). As an article or impersonal neuter pronoun, from Latin illud, the neuter singular of ille. Compare Portuguese o.

ety.text: From Middle English hymself, from Old English him selfum. Equivalent to him + -self.

senses.d: Him; the male object of a verb or preposition that also appears as the subject
ex: He injured himself.

senses.d: He; used as an intensifier, often to emphasize that the referent is the exclusive participant in the predicate
ex: He was injured himself.
Therefore the Lord himſelfe ſhal giue you a ſigne:[…].

senses.d: The subject or non-reflexive object of a predicate; he himself.
ex: With shame remembers, while himself was one / Of the same herd, himself the same had done.
Yet it is that himselfe had been liberally gratified by his Unkle with militarie rewards, before ever he went to warres.

senses.d: The subject or non-reflexive object of a predicate; he (used of upper-class gentlemen, or sarcastically, of men who imagine themselves to be more important than others)
ex: Has himself come down to breakfast yet?
Have you seen himself yet this morning?
